If I trace the dots back to how I landed in my current job, it's someone who I met years before I had any LinkedIn-related question for her. Actually before LinkedIn was even a company.

This morning on Today, I mentioned how relationships were integral to my own career as a way of talking about how essential networking is for all of us. Whether you think you may want a new job now or down the road, want to change careers, or are just getting started, networking is critical.

But it's also terrifying. In a recent survey, we found that 63% of people say they’ve never been taught this essential business skill, and the #1 reason people hesitate to reach out is fearing they’ll waste someone's time.

My message: You aren't wasting their time, and networking isn't as transactional or uncomfortable as it sounds. 85% of people actually want to give back and offer advice.

A few simple ways to make networking feel less intimidating and far more effective:
• Widen your definition: You're probably already networking without realizing it—whether chatting with colleagues or connecting on the sidelines of a kids' sports game.
• Gamify in-person events: If you hate entering rooms where you don't know anyone, do what I do and set a challenge to meet two new people before you allow yourself to leave.
• Engage genuinely online: Leaving thoughtful comments on posts makes you 3x more likely to receive a connection request and 5x more likely to get an inbound email.
• Be hyper-specific with your asks: Never, ever say, "Can I pick your brain?" Instead, state specifically why them, what you hope to learn, and ask for a focused 10 minutes.
• Maintain the connection: Only 27% of professionals regularly maintain their network. Stay in touch by celebrating their achievements or sharing helpful updates, rather than only reaching out when you need a favor.

Oh, and thanks Shannon Brayton for getting me here :)

post.text:
AI is helping mathematicians make real progress on Navier-Stokes. A problem that has resisted humans for generations.

Super cool. But that’s not how a billion people are going to decide if AI matters.

They’re going to decide it matters when it gives them time back. When Sunday night isn’t spent doing expense reports. When a five-step approval becomes one step. When a doctor catches a disease earlier. When a kid anywhere in the world gets access to a great teacher. When healthcare gets better and more affordable.

Kevin Scott put it this way:
“A.I. is one of the most powerful things humans have ever invented for improving the quality of life of everyone, but it will take time. It should take time. We've always tackled super-challenging problems through technology. And so, we can either tell ourselves a good story about the future or a bad story about the future, and, whichever one we choose, that's probably the one that'll come true.”

The question is what we choose to do with it.

I think the best companies start with a vision: What is the world we want this technology to help create?

Then work backwards... Build toward that vision AND put the safeguards in place to do it responsibly.

The answer isn’t to start from fear, or to ignore the risks. It’s to be clear about the future we want, and build toward it with safeguards from the start.

This is a time for real leadership. Technical brilliance matters enormously. But so do judgment, experience, empathy, and an understanding of how businesses and institutions actually work, and how change actually lands on people.

The technology isn’t going to decide what kind of future we build with it. We will.

Today we're launching Exceeds Ink, the intelligence engine that turns every AI coding session into a signal you can run your engineering org on.

AI changed how engineers work faster than the measurement layer could keep up. Leaders are paying a fortune for these legacy signals, fueled by surveys, agent self-scores, or PR-level metadata. Low-confidence, lagging by weeks, blind to the coding session itself. 

Meanwhile the practices change every month and the spend climbs every week (thanks tokenmaxxing!). Leaders need high-confidence signal at the level the work is happening, fast enough to act on. They also need actionable insights from partners who are responding as fast as the tools are evolving, not just once a year.

Exceeds Ink is our new companion to the Exceeds platform that provides insights on agentic workflows from prompt to PR to action. High confidence signals. No more guessing.

Ink is built from the feedback in hundreds of conversations with engineering leaders, and aims to answers their most urgent asks:

1) What did we actually get for spending all this money on AI? 
Exceeds Ink shows cross-tool spend by team, feature, and workflow, tied to the prompts and PRs that produced shipping outcomes. Combined with our ticketing data integrations, it's ROI you can take to the board.

2) Are we getting meaningfully better or faster as we adopt? 
Exceeds Ink illuminates code quality, throughput, and cycle-time trends by team, paired with the AI behaviors driving each change.

3) Which teams are ready for bigger challenges, and which need coaching? Exceeds Ink brings local level, team and org-level insights. Who's getting 2x output, who's stuck, where managers should invest support.

4) What are the best techniques from our most impactful engineers, and how do we help the rest of the team adopt them? 
Exceeds Ink shares the prompt patterns, tools, and workflows your top performers are running. It analyzes and coaches in the sessions and workflow, and helps you roll-out the best practices by next sprint.

Exceeds Ink captures every session locally across Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, and Windsurf, reads the code each session produced, and links prompt to commit to outcome. Not a survey. Not an agent grading itself. 

Your source and prompts stay under your data controls.  Every day, the practices that work get captured, taught, and replicated. Every day, the org gets better.

Why "Ink?" Agents write, and most of that writing happens invisibly. Ink is the trace of it: what was drafted, what shipped, what was worth the tokens.

Exceeds Ink is available to our Enterprise customers today. To learn more or get a demo, visit us at https://www.exceeds.ai

post.text:
Everybody wants the moment.
Nobody talks about being on the wrong side of it.

Last week, I had two game-winning shots hit on me.
And yeah… that’s the part no one signs up for.

But it comes with the job.

When your role is to be a defender, to take on those matchups, to be trusted in the biggest moments… you’re also accepting the risk that sometimes, it won’t go your way. That’s part of it.

You don’t get to choose when those moments find you.
You only get to choose if you’re willing to step into them.

In most careers, failure is private.
In sports, it’s public, loud,  and immediate.

But avoiding failure often just means avoiding responsibility.
And I’d rather be the one in the play than watching it.

Because being trusted in those moments means you’ve earned your way there. And over time, continuing to show up in those situations is what separates you in the end. 

The outcome doesn’t always validate the process in the short term.
But the willingness to keep stepping into those moments… that’s where growth actually happens.

In business, it’s no different.

The people who grow the fastest are the ones willing to take the shot, own the outcome, and step back in again.

The moment doesn’t define you, your response to it does.

Sometimes people just hit tough shots. That's life.

post.text:
There’s new data out showing an increase in job openings for software engineers. This is counterintuitive for some, which is why there’s a paradox named after it. But if you lower the cost of something that was previously supply constrained, demand for that thing goes up. Software engineering is just one of the easiest examples to contemplate.

The process goes like this: every small business, every IT team, every large enterprise sees that engineering can now drive vastly more output. They then start to consider all the new things they can build or automate. They even test building prototypes themselves.

They only get so far with that approach because they realize there are still 50 other tasks that go into building software and maintaining it. So they start to hire more engineers to do that work. All of this for work they never would have considered automating or having software for if AI didn’t exist.

So yes, automating tasks, in plenty of fields (not all!), will lead to demand for experts, not less.

Designers spend so much time learning how to create intuitive, visually compelling products.
Then we apply for internships with plain-text resumes.

Lately, I’ve been experimenting with redesigning my resume as a set of architectural drawings. Architecture regularly condenses large amounts of information into systems that are still readable: axonometric sections, floor plans, diagrams, and annotations. I wanted to see what would happen if I applied that same logic to representing my experiences.

This isn’t meant to replace a portfolio, as portfolios are essential for showing how designers think and work. Instead, this is an exploration of whether the resume itself can also function as a designed object that communicates structure, hierarchy, and narrative at a glance.

Still very much a work in progress, but I’ve enjoyed treating the resume as a design problem rather than a form to fill out. Curious if either design resonates more and why. Feedback welcome!

post.text:
The person I most connected with in 2025 was none other than LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. 

But my most serendipitous connection with him was actually in an elevator in our San Francisco office during the afternoon lunch rush. 

I had 30 seconds to tell Ryan about my latest and favorite project on LinkedIn — launching a series of monthly live shows that are eligible for continuing nursing or medical education credit. 

The next thing I knew, Ryan featured my project in our company all-hands (I’m not supposed to share what happens in all-hands, but let’s just say he called it a “genius” idea — and it is. If you’re interested in being notified of future shows, let me know so I can add you to our distribution list.)

And starting very shortly, you’ll see a whole CE-eligible library of content on LinkedIn Learning (thank you to my LiL partner on this project, Almeera Jiwa Pratt!)

2025 was definitely a highlight of my time at LinkedIn. Thank you to my manager Devin Banerjee and our executive editor Laura Lorenzetti for giving me the runway to build something special this year.  

#YearinReview

post.text:
After 15 incredible years at LinkedIn, I'm closing this chapter with a heart full of gratitude. Moments of transition are naturally moments of reflection (and admittedly some anxiety about what comes next!), and I wanted to share a few themes that have stood out as I look back at my time at this extraordinary company: 

It has always been about the people.  In the moments that matter, colleagues have stood up, said a thing, committed to a feature, added a measurement - and ultimately these are the decisions that have mattered the most in our collective commitment to ensure that two people with equal talent have equal access to opportunity.

We are all better together. Sharing a piece of knowledge, questioning an insight (constructively), and leading with curiosity helps all of us either change our mind or sharpen our conviction as we all try to build a better world of work for everyone.  

People want to help people. This is what has stood out the most for me. The thousands of acts of kindness and generosity reflects the humility we all have that none of us got where we are alone - and some of us had a headstart.  Regardless, we are here to help each other every step of the way.  

An ask:  like many of us, I have taken dozens if not hundreds of leadership trainings over the years. There is one that continues to stand out - it is the “Crazy dancing man”.  It is worth watching the 3 min TED talk that captures the essence.  But if you don’t - here it is in a nutshell.  It is the “First Follower” that matters most. They are the ones that turn the lone nut into a leader.  So when you find a lone nut doing something extraordinary, find the courage to be that first follower…because that may truly make all the difference in the world. https://lnkd.in/gbD98FnM

To my fellow LinkedIn colleagues - thanks for always getting up and dancing with the team, for staying focused on the "every" in our vision statement and for saying yes to a LI Coaches opportunity. 

To the LinkedIn community - I am in awe of your generosity. Thanks for showing up, reaching out, connecting with the fellow jobseeker who needs a word of encouragement or an intro to someone in your network.  And a special plug this week (Giving Tuesday) to help amplify the amazing work about your favorite nonprofit.

Finally, to the Social Impact team and their new leader - this next chapter may be the most critical.  I could not have more confidence in each of you to lead the way to ensure that the world is better off because LinkedIn is in it.

post.text:
An underdiscussed phenomena that is starting to happen in organizations: AI-driven role conflict.

The roles in charge of design, product management, coding, marketing, etc. in a project used to have relatively clear lines. AI lets entrepreneurial workers extend into other roles and accelerate work, but there are no good templates to follow. Everyone can now code a little, design a little, market a little - what does that mean?

The result so far has been a mix of acceleration and retrenchment. Some cases I hear about, this gets bogged down in defense of existing roles ("how dare the marketer show me a product prototype when they can't even code and are just using AI") and in others, organizations start to rethink old teams and experiment.

post.text:
A few feature requests the LinkedIn team should consider: 

1) Extend the character limit on posts. No reason to have a policy that limits the time that users spend on the platform. 

2) Allow users to see "post saves." One of the best ways to understand the value of content you create is how many people save the content for later. 

3) A creator's comment to their own post should always the first one people see. If I provide additional thoughts to my post in the comments, it shouldn't be buried. 

4) Allow for in-post image embedding & simple text edits (bolding, italics). A more rich text post experience is more engaging for users & keeps them on-platform longer.

post.text:
Eleven years ago, in a meeting, Jeff Weiner sketched three intersecting circles to describe the qualities of people he most enjoyed working with. That simple image has quietly defined our company for years. It’s on our walls, our swag, and in our stories... It's cited frequently in interviews, offsites, and all-hands...

Today, we’re making it official as LinkedIn’s culture statement. We dream big, we get sh*t done, and we know how to have fun,

As I shared at our Company Kickoff:

Dream big means pushing boundaries. While the phrase may sound familiar, here’s what it must mean for us: true ambition isn’t about chasing big numbers or vague goals. It’s about forming sharp points of view, testing them boldly, and discovering something fundamentally new. Growth matters, but it should be the result of breakthroughs, not the goal itself. Dreaming big at LinkedIn means imagining the breakthrough that redefines what’s possible and proving it in 6, 12, or 18 months. Not “get this to 100M users fast,” but “make it work beautifully for the right 10K in two months.” Learn something so true and valuable that scale becomes inevitable.

Get sh*t done means execution still matters. Vision without follow-through is vapor. Dreaming big is essential, but without delivery, it’s just pie in the sky.

Know how to have fun means we bring joy and humanity into the work, because without that, what’s the point? The phrase “knowing how to have fun” is a proxy for people that share values, and people who are aligned in terms of how they want to go about their work. Very important – it’s not “have fun”, work isn’t a party. It’s “know how to have fun” - people who want to be around one another, who don't take themselves too seriously.

The real power, though, is at the intersection. The people who dream big and execute. Who move fast and bring others along. Who inspire ambition and make space for levity. Those are the people who define the personality of LinkedIn. And they are the culture we want and need to scale​.

And when I take a step back - that image captures exactly what the world needs from us all right now. It captures how we need to think about our members, our customers, and how we stand up to support them. For 22 years, we have always done it. And We will continue to do it.

Jeff's original post: https://lnkd.in/gC6VPSTR

Celebrating my 18th year as a LinkedIn employee.

18 years ago, I joined #LinkedIn, a company with a mission to help professionals become more productive and successful. We were in startup mode, chasing a goal to connect talent with opportunity at scale, and a vision to create economic opportunity for every member of the global workforce.

What started as a bold vision has become one of the greatest company success stories of our generation - transforming how the world connects, hires, learns, and sells.

18 Years at LinkedIn Taught Me about Impact that Lasts ... Growth, Trust, and the Privilege to Help Others Succeed.

During that time, I launched a brand and products to market, wrote the LinkedIn sales playbook, created the LinkedIn sales coaching program, generated hundreds of millions in revenue, and scaled global initiatives - but my proudest moments are in the lives changed, the intelligent risks taken, and the careers and businesses launched because someone dared to click "Connect."

Thank you, all of you, for being one of LinkedIn's 1 Billion+ members … and thank you for letting me be part of your story, your growth, and your pursuit of something bigger.

#ActLikeAnOwner #TakeIntelligentRisks #MembersFirst #RelationshipsMatter #BeOpenHonestAndConstructive #DemandExcellence

post.text:
Five years in.
 
When I stepped into this role, I brought experience, purpose, and a deep belief in the power of people. What I've gained since then is harder to measure: more humility, more clarity and a stronger appreciation for how complex and how human this work really is.
 
Have I made mistakes? Yep. Some small, and some that still make me cringe. But each one has taught me something important about what it means to lead with intention. Leadership, I've learned, is about listening deeply, staying grounded, and showing up honestly even when you're not sure what to do next (especially when everyone is looking to you for a brilliant solution).
 
Over these five years, I've had the privilege of working alongside extraordinary people. Together, we've supported employees through times of uncertainty, helped people thrive at work, and tried to make things just a little simpler, more human, and more meaningful.
 
We've worked to build a community where people can show up fully, do their best work, and deepen the relationships that make it all worth it. We've brought in amazing talent, supported real change, and tried to keep things moving forward even when the world felt sideways.
 
I'm also deeply grateful for a team that brings passion, sharp thinking, and laughter into every room. And for a boss who pushes me to stretch my thinking. 
 
If you're thinking about a future in HR, I've learned that design thinking and change leadership matter more than ever. The best teammates are those who remove roadblocks, make things simpler and look for elegant, human solutions. Always listening, observing and leading with heart.
 
Here's to five years of learning, unlearning and building something meaningful together.

comment.comment: Steven Joseph Evelyn did you just message the CEO of LinkedIn asking if he’s looking for a job 🤣

post.text:
Fourteen years ago this week I walked into a small office in Dublin to join a mid-size startup that was rapidly expanding across Europe. With less than 30 million members and 150 colleagues across the region, never could I have imagined how life enhancing and career defining that moment would be. 

Now, with more than 560 million members in EMEA & LATAM and 1000s of colleagues across 14 offices, it’s amazing to see how far the business has come.

Earlier today, I shared the news with my team that I have decided to leave LinkedIn at the end of June. From helping scale the European ads business and being our EMEA & LATAM Managing Director, to leading our global enterprise ads business, and sponsoring our LGBTQ+ ERG, working at LinkedIn has been one of the biggest privileges of my life.

I have spent fourteen years surrounded by the smartest, kindest, funniest, most resilient and most determined group of people I’ve ever met. To the LinkedIn team, to our customers and to our members, thank you from the bottom of my heart. 

Working at a company that is at the intersection of doing well and doing good, and which helps seven people a minute find a job feels immensely rewarding. If you can find that special combination at some point in your life, go and grab it.

After 25 years of working almost every day, I’ve decided to take a ‘gap year’. My plan is to travel, brush up on my Italian, do a diving course, and spend some quality time with family and friends. For those that know me well, switching off is not my forte, but I’m going to give it my best shot! When I’m ready, I will figure out my next chapter.

When I step away from the business, I’m delighted to share that my brilliant colleague, Sue Duke, will take on the role of Managing Director, LinkedIn EMEA & LATAM, in addition to her responsibilities as LinkedIn’s VP Global Public Policy & Economic Graph. I’ve had the pleasure of working with Sue for 10+ years and have seen first-hand her incredible intellect, her empathetic leadership style, and her boundless optimism for LinkedIn’s potential. I’m excited for our team, customers and members to experience her goodness first hand. 

Congratulations Sue - you’re going to thrive in your new role!
